title: I Said Palantir Stock Would Top $220 This Year. Here's What It Has to Prove on Nov. 2.
detail:
I Said Palantir Stock Would Top $220 This Year. Here's What It Has to Prove on Nov. 2.
Patrick Sanders, The Motley Fool
Sun, October 25, 2026 at 10:03 AM PDT 5 min read
PLTR
NVDA
Explore stocks on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

Back in August, I made a bullish prediction about Palantir Technologies (NASDAQ: PLTR): I said the artificial intelligence (AI) software company would reach $220 per share before the end of 2026, driven by its outstanding revenue growth and increasing demand from commercial customers.

I'm sticking with that prediction. But Palantir has some work to do.

Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 14x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue »

On Friday, shares were trading in the $190 to $198 range, leaving the stock roughly 11% to 16% below my target. And with Palantir scheduled to report third-quarter earnings on Nov. 2, investors are about to get a much better idea of whether my prediction will come true.

I think Palantir needs to deliver three things to make a run at $220.

Image source: Getty Images.
1. Quarterly revenue needs to top $2.3 billion

Palantir has established a remarkable track record of accelerating revenue growth, thanks largely to businesses adopting its Artificial Intelligence Platform (AIP).

Second-quarter revenue jumped 93% year over year to $1.94 billion. U.S. commercial revenue was particularly impressive, climbing 149% to $764 million, while U.S. government revenue increased 90% to $809 million. Those are outstanding numbers for a company of Palantir's size.

But management's third-quarter revenue guidance of approximately $2.16 billion implies sequential growth of roughly 12%, compared with about 19% in the second quarter. That seems awfully conservative to me.

Palantir has consistently beaten its revenue guidance this year, and another quarter of 19% sequential growth would put revenue at approximately $2.3 billion.

That's the number I'm watching. If Palantir's revenue is growing at an accelerating rate, that would be an important bullish signal to the market.

2. Sales tied to the company's AI sovereignty efforts must increase

One of Palantir's more interesting opportunities involves the market for AI sovereignty services -- helping organizations maintain control over their data and AI operations rather than surrendering much of that control to external technology providers. It has been a primary focus of CEO Alex Karp in recent months.

It's a natural fit for Palantir. The company's software already helps customers connect their data, build digital models of their operations, and deploy AI applications while maintaining control over sensitive information.

Palantir has used its client boot camps to demonstrate how its software can solve potential customers' operational problems. Its sovereignty-focused efforts offer another way to introduce organizations to those capabilities.

But there's an important distinction between demonstrating what software can do and getting customers to pay for it. In the Q3 report, I will be looking for fresh evidence that these efforts are producing meaningful business. That could include new contracts, larger customer commitments, or management providing specific information about how sovereignty-related demand is contributing to growth.

Palantir's commercial business has already been expanding rapidly. Showing that its sovereignty initiatives are generating additional revenue would give investors another reason to believe that growth can continue.

3. Sterling profit margins must get even better

Revenue growth gets most of the attention when Palantir reports earnings. But profitability deserves just as much scrutiny.

Palantir reported an adjusted operating margin of 62% in the second quarter, up from 60% in the first quarter. That's an extraordinary level of profitability for a software company that's growing as quickly as Palantir.

It also raises expectations.

One of the advantages of selling software is that revenue can grow much faster than expenses once the company has developed its products and infrastructure. That allows a larger fraction of each incremental sale to be converted into operating profit.

I'd like to see Palantir push its adjusted operating margin above 62% in the third quarter. If revenue growth continues to accelerate while margins expand, it would strengthen the argument that Palantir will eventually justify its currently expensive valuation.

Can Palantir reach $220 in 2026?

I'm still bullish on Palantir. Its AIP has become an increasingly important tool for businesses that are looking to put AI to work, and its financial results have supported that enthusiasm.

But the stock isn't cheap, and investors have already priced in tremendous expected growth.

That's why the Nov. 2 report matters so much.

Revenue above $2.3 billion, evidence of meaningful business from AI sovereignty, and another improvement in operating margins would make a compelling case that Palantir's business momentum hasn't peaked.

I don't expect Palantir stock will reach $220 this year simply because management delivers another good earnings report. It needs to give investors a reason to raise their expectations.

But if Palantir delivers on all three of these points, I think my prediction has a good chance of coming true.

Here's What a $10,000 Investment in Palantir Could Be Worth in 10 Years
Jennifer Saibil, The Motley Fool

Palantir Technologies (NASDAQ: PLTR) has been one of the most successful artificial intelligence (AI) stocks on the market. It's up more than 1,000% over the past three years, although it's up only a modest 10% year-to-date, roughly in line with the S&P 500.

If you were lucky enough to invest $10,000 in Palantir stock on its first day of trading in 2020, you'd have around $212,000 today. But where could a $10,000 investment today possibly take you?

Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 14x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue »

Why Palantir is one of the hottest AI stocks

Palantir is different from most other hot AI stocks because it doesn't make any of the parts, like Nvidia or Micron, and it doesn't support the build-out, like CoreWeave or Bloom Energy. Instead, it uses AI to help organizations and businesses unify different databases to detect patterns and make informed decisions.

Palantir's platform gives users an edge over the competition, and it's attracting more and more business as clients see real value. At some point, it's going to become the baseline for working, because it will be hard to compete without it.

It also has a unique working model. It customizes each client's interface based on its unique needs, and either brings in the company's team for a "bootcamp" or, in certain cases, sends its own engineers into a client's business.

Image source: The Motley Fool.

Palantir has several products. Its original platform, Gotham, was created to help defense and law enforcement analyze data, while Foundry does similar things for commercial enterprises. Its Artificial Intelligence Platform (AIP) brings AI models and agents into the operations to pull it all together.

Growth has been spectacular as organizations realize what these kinds of features can do for them. Total revenue increased 93% year over year in the second quarter, driven by a 149% increase in the U.S. commercial business, which now accounts for 81% of the business. It closed 220 deals worth at least $1 million and 73 deals worth at least $10 million, all of which are multiyear contracts that generate annual revenue.

It's also highly profitable. The adjusted operating margin was 62% in the quarter, and earnings per share (EPS) increased from $0.13 to $0.41.

Risks and opportunities

How much higher can it go? The market obviously thinks a lot more, considering how expensive the stock is. It trades at a trailing P/E ratio of 167 and a price-to-sales ratio of 81, making it the most expensive stock in the S&P 500 by that metric.

There's an easy sales pitch for software that can help organizations run their vehicles and equipment more effectively: Show clients how the product can save time or money. Samsara (NYSE: IOT) does just that, helping to bridge the gap between operational data and software.

Artificial intelligence (AI) can make these tools even more productive, but greater productivity alone doesn't make an investment thesis. For investors looking ahead to 2027, the real question is whether Samsara can turn its potential into fundamental growth that exceeds the expectations embedded in its stock. If it can, it's possible that this under-the-radar stock could soar, perhaps even matching the run of Palantir, a stock that skyrocketed more than 700% during the past five years. Let's dig in and see how realistic that scenario is.

Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue »

Image source: Getty Images.
What Samsara actually does

To understand Samsara's business, we must follow a hypothetical example. Imagine a factory. Tens of thousands of moving parts and hundreds of workers are hard at work, focused on the task at hand. There's one problem: A key piece of equipment is at risk of failure. Worse, this type of failure wouldn't just cause downtime; it could also pose a health and safety risk. Samsara's software is designed to catch these issues before they become critical. It keeps operations running smoothly, saves money, and protects key assets.

The company operates on a "land-and-expand" model. It sells its product platform once, then collects recurring revenue from clients. A key aspect of its business model is upselling -- selling additional modules to existing customers to generate more revenue.

Can 2027 be Samsara's breakout year?

As for fundamentals, they've taken off recently. Samsara's revenue has increased from about $250 million in 2021 to more than $1.84 billion during the past 12 months. Free cash flow has also increased, swinging from about $150 million in cash burn in 2023 to $255 million in free cash flow during the past 12 months. What's more, the company recently turned the corner on profitability, generating about $91 million in net income during the past year.

Although these metrics are encouraging, Samsara will need to go further in 2027 for its stock to truly take off. The company recently noted that roughly 96% of its customers with more than $100,000 in annual recurring revenue (ARR) now use at least two of its products, and 70% use three or more. If the company can increase those numbers further while expanding its existing customer base, the stock market could take notice.

Shares of Palantir Technologies (NASDAQ:PLTR) ended at a record $209.05 on Oct. 9. At roughly $198 as I write, they're about 5% under that peak.

The artificial intelligence (AI) software specialist's second-quarter revenue grew 93% year over year to about $1.94 billion. And management now expects about $8.15 billion in revenue for 2026, or 82% more than last year.

Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 14x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue »

At this rate, a $10 billion year isn't far away. Palantir's revenue for its past four quarters could clear that level as early as the middle of 2027.

My prediction: when it does, Palantir stock will trade at roughly $208, almost exactly where it set its record. That'd be just about 5% above today's price, though Palantir would be taking in about 60% more revenue a year than it did in its past four reported quarters.

Image source: Getty Images.

When does Palantir reach $10 billion?

Palantir's growth has sped up for four straight quarters. Revenue climbed 48% year over year in the second quarter of 2025, then 63% in the third quarter, 70% in the fourth quarter, 85% in the first quarter of 2026, and 93% in the second quarter. Net income grew even faster, more than tripling year over year to around $1.06 billion in the second quarter.

Management's guidance, though, calls for growth to slow from here. Palantir sees third-quarter revenue of around $2.16 billion, or about 83% growth. And its full-year outlook implies fourth-quarter revenue of around $2.42 billion, up about 72%. Then again, Palantir has tended to beat its own forecasts. In each of the past three quarters, revenue landed around 6% to 8% above the top of management's range.

Plus, the full-year target keeps rising. It went from around $7.19 billion in February to about $7.65 billion in May, then to around $8.15 billion in August.

If the third and fourth quarters match guidance, Palantir's trailing revenue reaches $10 billion when its first-half 2027 sales rise around 52% year over year. If those two quarters beat guidance by about as much as the past three did, growth in the mid-40s would do it.

Either way, the milestone would probably show up in Palantir's second-quarter 2027 report.

Investors are paying less for each dollar of sales

Palantir's market value of around $477 billion comes out to about 77 times its revenue in the past four reported quarters. A year ago, the price-to-sales multiple was about 128 times sales. The sales multiple fell by around 40% in a stretch when revenue growth almost doubled.

Palantir Technologies (PLTR:NASDAQ) stock is up 17.2% since early January, closing at $196.75 on October 23. That return hides how the year actually went. On August 3, the stock sat 25.2% below where the period began, by my math, and a single session after the company's second-quarter report did most of the repair work.

Palantir stock jumped 29.45% on August 4 and went on to set a record close of $209.05 in October. The business never had a bad quarter along the way. The price did.

Why Palantir Stock Sank While the Numbers Climbed
PLTR Stock Price Return: Year to Date (TIKR)

The first leg down came in January and February, as software stocks sold off on fears that AI could disrupt the sector, a link Barron's drew directly for Palantir. The company's own February 2 report didn't stop it. Fourth-quarter revenue came in at $1.407 billion, ahead of the $1.329 billion IBES estimate, but the stock gave back its early pop within days.

May followed the same script. First-quarter revenue rose 85% to $1.633 billion, U.S. revenue growth crossed 100% for the first time, and management lifted full-year guidance to $7.65 billion to $7.662 billion. Shares kept drifting lower.

The bottom came in late June. Palantir stock lost 20.4% in a seven-session losing streak from June 16 to June 25, closing at $107.27. That was its low for the period and 36.1% below where January started. The rebound began on June 26 with a 5.28% gain. The following Monday, June 29, Palantir announced a strategic initiative with Nvidia (NVDA:NASDAQ) to run Nvidia AI and Nemotron open models in sovereign environments, aimed at U.S. government agencies. Palantir Technologies (NASDAQ: PLTR) stock has been on an incredible run. While the stock's gain of roughly 13.5% is roughly in line with the rally for the S&P 500 (SNPINDEX: ^GSPC), the artificial intelligence (AI) software specialist has absolutely crushed the market on a longer timeline.

Over the last five years, Palantir stock has risen roughly 714%. Meanwhile, the S&P 500's level has climbed 70.5%. With Palantir now trading at roughly $200 per share, is it likely that the company is gearing up for a stock split in the near future?

Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue »

Image source: Getty Images.
Don't count on a stock split just yet

In recent years, stock splits have become highly anticipated, closely watched market events -- and for good reason. The announcements and implementations of splits have coincided with substantial valuation gains for many companies that have implemented them.

A stock split doesn't alter a business's fundamentals. It simply cuts the pie that is a company's share count into a larger number of pieces.

As a result, the stock price is reduced by a corresponding ratio. While this doesn't improve the underlying business, the lower share price has often made shares more attractive to retail investors. In turn, increased buying action pushes the stock higher. Palantir has yet to conduct a stock split across its roughly six-year history as a publicly traded company.

While I think there's a good chance additional share price gains will prompt the company to split within the next few years, I don't think there's anything to suggest a split is imminent. Trading at roughly $200 per share, Palantir stock isn't yet at a pure-dollar pricing level that's likely to spur a split.

If the stock approaches $500 per share and continues to show strength at that level, I think a split becomes much more likely. That's a level that is historically more likely to encourage stock splits.

So for investors hoping that a near-term stock split will help push Palantir stock higher, I don't think that's a solid bet. The good news is that Palantir doesn't have to rely on a stock split to boost its valuation.

In its second-quarter report published in August, Palantir announced that sales grew 93% year over year to $1.935 billion. Meanwhile, non-GAAP (generally accepted accounting principles) adjusted operating income came in at $1.194 billion -- good for a 62% margin.

Palantir is growing sales at an incredible pace and posting margins that are extremely impressive, even by the standards of high-margin software companies. These characteristics could continue to support bullish momentum for the stock.

title: You Might Be Able to Invest in the Starlab Space Station -- but Should You?
detail:
You Might Be Able to Invest in the Starlab Space Station -- but Should You?
Rich Smith, The Motley Fool
Sat, October 24, 2026 at 5:28 AM PDT 5 min read
VOYG
SPCX
LDOS
NOC
PLTR
Explore stocks on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

After more than a quarter-century in service, the International Space Station is ready for its last hurrah. Sometime after 2030, the space agency plans to pay Elon Musk's SpaceX $850 million to push ISS out of orbit and into the ocean. It's sad news -- but here's the good news:

America is building a new international space station, this time owned and operated by private companies -- private international companies -- to replace ISS. Several teams are competing for the honor, with pole position likely held by Starlab, a consortium led by Voyager Technologies (NYSE: VOYG) and including partners such as Hilton Worldwide, Leidos, Northrop Grumman, and Palantir.

Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 14x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue »

And now here's (potentially) the best part: You may be able to invest in Starlab directly.

Image source: Getty Images.
How to buy a space station in three easy steps

Rumors are circulating regarding an effort to raise $300 million in "Series A" funding for the Starlab joint venture. Series A is the term of art for the first major funding round after a start-up company has exhausted its "seed capital" financing. Multiple institutional investors have already confirmed they're contributing capital to the funding round. If you're looking for an opportunity to get in on the "ground floor" of a space station company -- this may be it.

But "getting in" might not be easy. To participate in Starlab's funding round (assuming it happens), you first need to find a private investment company that has been invited to participate. I personally know of one such company, but don't have permission to name it publicly -- so I won't. (But it is out there.)

Next, you need to find out the price.

Starlab is seeking to raise $300 million by selling "preferred units" (not exactly stock, but similar) in the joint venture. Each unit is reportedly valued near $90,000, and the company as a whole is valued at $950 million prior to the Series A (and could be worth $1.25 billion afterward).

Finally, you should decide if that price is "worth it."

Should you invest (if you can)?

For me, that's the real question, because I'm not convinced investing directly in the Starlab joint venture is the best route -- even if that's an option for you.

Consider: Starlab has received $211 million in grant funding from NASA, and a further $15 million from the Texas Space Commission, plus tens of millions in capital contributions from several of its joint venture partners. But according to the latest data from S&P Global Market Intelligence, Starlab has no revenue -- much less profit -- yet. That's not surprising, seeing as the joint venture hasn't yet built or launched the space station it needs to generate the revenue -- but it does raise the risk of investing in Starlab.

Starlab probably won't begin generating revenue until after its space station reaches orbit, which is scheduled for no earlier than 2029, and cannot happen until SpaceX makes a Starship rocket available for launch. Starlab does, however, have $500 million in commercial reservations from potential customers, and says there's pent-up demand for further contracts.

Whether that's enough demand to justify the estimated $2.8 billion to $3.3 billion it will cost to build and launch the station -- and earn a profit -- remains to be seen.

A better way to invest in Starlab?

For now, there's not much transparency around an investment in the Starlab joint venture. And for this reason, it may make sense for individual investors to focus instead on investing in one or more of the publicly traded companies that comprise the Starlab joint venture. Those, at least, must file financial statements with the SEC, giving investors a clearer view of their path to profitability.

Thinking along this line, the most logical stock to consider investing in is Voyager, the company leading the development of Starlab.

Mind you, Voyager isn't profitable either. But it does have revenue -- about $174 million generated over the past year, primarily from its defense and national security division. At a recent market capitalization of just over $1.5 billion, that means Voyager stock has an 8.9 times price-to-sales ratio.

That isn't cheap for a space stock -- yet. But analysts have Voyager pegged for more than $291 million in total sales through the end of this year, rising to $518 million next year, and $982 million the year after that. By 2029, the earliest date we might expect to see Starlab in orbit, they predict Voyager will be doing nearly $1.9 billion in annual sales -- and finally earn its first profit.

Assuming you can wait that long, then today's valuation of less than 1x 2029 sales could be cheap enough to make Voyager stock a winning investment.

Image source: The Motley Fool.
Palantir's AI business is booming

Palantir originally started off offering its AI platform to government entities. This was an incredibly popular offering, and Palantir's government contracts still make up the majority of its revenue stream today. However, Palantir also expanded to the commercial side of the business, and it's seeing huge adoption of its AI platform.

Essentially, Palantir is an AI platform that plugs into existing data streams and helps derive actionable insights. Through automation, Palantir can also assist in deploying AI agents that do tasks on behalf of its users. Palantir's platform dramatically improves the efficiency of one person in their role and can provide decision-making capabilities that far exceed what a human can deliver.

Companies and governments are adopting Palantir's software at a breathtaking pace, which is evidenced by its 93% revenue growth rate in Q2. U.S. commercial revenue grew even faster, with revenue from this segment increasing at a 149% pace. AI adoption is happening rapidly, and Palantir is one of the companies that's taking market share.

One of the biggest surprises with Palantir is how great its margins are. New headlines are filled with stories about how quickly some AI firms are growing, but also highlight that they're spending far more than they make. Palantir isn't in that boat, as it delivered an impressive 55% profit margin in Q2.

It doesn't get better than that, but this also opens up a new problem.

Palantir's stock is pricey

Palantir's stock is one of the more expensive on the market, and it trades for almost 125 times this year's earnings.

title: Palantir stock faces brutal test after crushing expectations
detail:
Palantir stock faces brutal test after crushing expectations
Faizan Farooque, Celine Provini
Fri, October 23, 2026 at 6:47 PM PDT 7 min read
PLTR
Trade PLTR on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

Palantir Technologies (PLTR) has created a problem most companies would love to have: Wall Street now expects it to crush expectations.

MarketBeat expects $2.18 billion in revenue and 41 cents per share from the AI software company's third-quarter results after the market closes Nov. 2. Revenue would increase 84% year over year.

Palantir's own prediction is less optimistic. Wall Street has successfully factored another beat into its expectations ahead of the report, as management guided for $2.160 billion to $2.164 billion in sales.

This disparity contributes to the explanation of an odd division among experts.

Citi raised its Palantir price target to $250 from $245 on Oct. 22 and expects U.S. commercial revenue to grow more than 140%, according to TipRanks.

But Investing.com, citing StoneX, reported that the firm maintained a Hold rating, even as it also expected a strong quarter. StoneX said investors may focus less on whether Palantir beats estimates than on how large the upside is.

Both companies anticipate Palantir's success. The point of contention is how much positive news investors should already anticipate.

Palantir's growth has made a beat the baseline

Investors have several reasons to expect even better results from Palantir.

Second-quarter revenue surged 93% year over year to $1.94 billion, while U.S. commercial revenue jumped 149% to $764 million. U.S. government revenue rose 90% to $809 million.

The company also closed 220 deals worth at least $1 million during the quarter, including 98 worth at least $5 million and 73 worth at least $10 million.

With adjusted free cash flow of $1.22 billion, the margin was 63%.

Palantir reported that U.S. commercial residual deal value, or contractual work that hasn't yet been recorded as revenue, increased 124% to $6.24 billion.

These figures complicate the value argument beyond just labeling Palantir as pricey.

Investors often expect that the company's growth will ultimately support an exceptionally high stock-market value. However, every extraordinary quarter also complicates the subsequent comparison.

Palantir raised its full-year revenue guidance after the second quarter to $8.150 billion to $8.158 billion, representing roughly 82% growth. It also expects U.S. commercial revenue to exceed $3.424 billion, or grow at least 134%.

Despite increasingly challenging year-earlier comparisons, Citi now anticipates that business will expand by more than 140% in the third quarter.

Citi's checks with Palantir partners showed strong demand across U.S. commercial and government businesses, according to TipRanks.

That makes U.S. commercial growth particularly important on Nov. 2. Palantir doesn't only need businesses to test its AI software. Customers must increase such deployments and continue to convert AI initiatives into bigger contracts to maintain the bull case.

Citi believes that is taking place, and StoneX doesn't contest the momentum.

The more difficult issue to assess is how much momentum Palantir's stock already reflects.

Palantir expects U.S. commercial revenue to exceed $3.424 billion, or grow at least 134%.John Lamparski / Getty Images
Palantir's valuation changes what counts as good

Palantir trades at 41.6 times its forecast 2027 enterprise value-to-revenue ratio, according to Investing.com.

For a Main Street investor, the implication matters more than the Wall Street terminology.

For every $1 in revenue that StoneX projects Palantir will make in 2027, investors are allocating almost $41 in enterprise value.

A 100% revenue growth company can command a higher multiple than a typical software company. When growth slows, large deals fall, or management lowers investor optimism, a high multiple means the market is less patient.

Palantir shares closed at $196.19 on Oct. 22, about 8% below their $212.94 52-week high. Investing.com shows 21 Buy ratings, nine Holds, and two Sells, with an average 12-month price target of $206.43.

Related: Palantir's Pentagon role reveals a surprising edge

That average implies only modest upside from the Oct. 22 close, even though some individual analysts see much more.

An excellent example is Citi's new $250 objective. In essence, the bank is making the case that Palantir can continue exceeding projections quickly enough to sustain further gains.

Investors are urged by StoneX's Hold recommendation to take into account the opposing viewpoint: Excellent performance alone can't warrant a new rating when a company already exhibits years of exceptional development.

As a result, Nov. 2 is more of an expectations test than a straightforward profits test.

Demand is genuine, according to Palantir's second-quarter data. Another concern that has to be addressed in the third quarter is whether demand can keep growing fast enough to outpace what investors have already factored in.

What Palantir has to prove on Nov. 2

The first criterion is the most straightforward. Revenue must meet Wall Street's standards, not just Palantir's.

The maximum amount recommended by management is $2.164 billion. About $2.18 billion is what analysts anticipate.

Therefore, a result that falls between those two figures may theoretically surpass Palantir's prediction while still disappointing investors.

Here, StoneX's caution over the magnitude of the upside becomes crucial.

U.S. commercial growth is the second test. The company's 149% second-quarter growth is one of the best indications that Palantir's AI potential is expanding beyond its long-standing government business and into corporate America.

Citi anticipates growth exceeding 140% once again. If Palantir produces anything at that rate, it will bolster the claim that companies are using its AI platform more widely rather than just testing it.

More Palantir:

Palantir's latest AI move reveals a much bigger ambition

Palantir faces a $330 million test U.S. investors should watch closely

UBS resets Palantir stock price target for the rest of 2026

Large contracts provide a third test.

Palantir closed 73 deals worth $10 million each in Q2. StoneX advised investors to watch large-deal activity and net retention, which measures whether existing customers are spending more.

These two figures approach the same problem in different ways. Gaining new clients is important, but Palantir's value increasingly demands that current clients expand their deployments while new clients sign more significant contracts.

Lastly, investors need to pay attention to what management says about the fourth quarter.

A significant third-quarter beat combined with a notably slower projection may swiftly divert focus from Palantir's recent achievements to the potential rate of growth normalization.

Overall, it can be the most significant figure that management provides to investors.

Palantir has already shown that there is a market for their AI software. It has not yet shown how long growth beyond 80%, 100%, or even 140% in some areas of the business can continue as the revenue base grows, since no company can do so in a single quarter.

Because of this difference, Citi and StoneX may both anticipate a strong quarter, even if they have conflicting opinions on the stock.

Investors do not need to act as if Palantir is inexpensive in the bull scenario. Palantir's performance must continue to make the current value seem less drastic over time.

The danger is almost identical to the mirror counterpart.

It is not necessary for Palantir's business to decline for the stock to suffer. Growth only has to fall short of the very high standards set by its prior success.

That is the real test on Nov. 2.

Although another strong quarter is anticipated for Palantir, it is unclear whether it will deliver another quarter that is strong enough to lead Wall Street to raise its expectations again.
